also: I’d like to introduce you to

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation; with an accusative of the person and a dative
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.5.3: tōtum dēnique hominem tibi ita trādō
Hor. Epist. 1.9.3: ut tibi sē laudāre et trādere cōner
terms.comment: Properly “hand over”: Cicero and Horace use it in letters introducing a friend to a great man (Cic. Fam. 7.5.3; Hor. Epist. 1.9.3). Traupman’s dialogue has velim trādere tibi cōnsōbrīnam meam, “I’d like to introduce my cousin to you”.

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation; with an accusative and a dative
evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.17.2: sīc eī tē commendāvī et trādidī
terms.comment: A letter of introduction is litterae commendāticiae (Cic. Fam. 5.5.1, Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: take (a young man) to a teacher or a patron
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation; with ad and the accusative
evidence: Cic. Amic. 1: ā patre ita eram dēductus ad Scaevolam
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to conduct a young man to a public teacher”.

phrases.latin: tōtum dēnique hominem tibi ita trādō, dē manū, ut ajunt, in manum tuam istam et victōriā et fidē praestantem
phrases.english: In short, I hand the whole man over to you, from my hand, as they say, into that hand of yours, so outstanding in victory and in good faith.

phrases.latin: Septimius, Claudī, nīmīrum intellegit ūnus, quantī mē faciās, nam cum rogat et prece cōgit scīlicet ut tibi sē laudāre et trādere cōner
phrases.english: Septimius, Claudius, is plainly the only one who knows how much you think of me: for he asks, and begs me, if you please, to try to commend and introduce him to you.

phrases.latin: ego autem ā patre ita eram dēductus ad Scaevolam sūmptā virīlī togā, ut, quoad possem et licēret, ā senis latere numquam discēderem
phrases.english: When I had put on the toga of manhood, my father took me to Scaevola, and so, as far as I could and was allowed, I never left the old man’s side.
I’d like to introduce you to my cousin.
